extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, and students of poetics / creative-writing students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and evaluating dramatic (tragedy) and epic poetry, focusing on plot, language, diction, metaphor, chorus, unity, and suitability of devices for stage or narration. Draws on classical (Aristotelian) criteria for excellence in poetic imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery of tragic forms
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should endeavour to excel in the several forms of tragedy (peripetia and discovery; the pathetic; the moral; and the simple), or at least in as many as possible and in those that are most esteemed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List of forms: tragedies depending on peripetia and discovery; the pathetic (like Ajax); the moral; and the simple (like Prometheus). Aim to master multiple forms rather than only one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge by plot and solution, not the fable
rubrics_metrics.description: The difference or sameness of one tragedy and another must not be estimated by the fable, but by the plot and solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many form the plot well and the solution ill; both plot and solution ought to be equally skilful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of action: avoid epic multiplicity in tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: It is necessary not to give a tragedy the form of an epic poem (i.e., one containing many fables); a drama should not attempt to represent an entire long narrative (e.g., whole Trojan War) in one play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of length and proportion, attempting the whole of a large epic subject on stage exceeds expected boundaries and has led to failure or poor reception (example: Agatho). Prefer selecting a part of the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single action and peripetia-friendly devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedies that depend on peripetia and have a single action often attain their purpose by means which appear wonderful and not only tragical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such surprising devices can be 'agreeable to our feelings' and need not be contrary to probability—Agatho notes that many things which seem improbable may nonetheless be probable. Use wondrous events if they produce pity/fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chorus as an actor contributing to action
rubrics_metrics.description: The chorus ought to be considered as one of the actors and should contribute to the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not in the manner used by Euripides (where sung parts often seem unrelated), but like Sophocles. Avoid introducing embolima (musical interludes) foreign to the subject or choral parts that have no relation to the fable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include peripetia, discovery, and pathos
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragedy (and, for dramatic effect, epic imitation) should have peripetia (reversal), discovery, and pathos, and the language and sentiment should be beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are essential components of tragic imitation and contribute to emotional effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentiment must perform rhetorical offices and work off-stage
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentiment in drama must use the same forms as rhetoric (to demonstrate, to refute, to excite the passions such as fear, anger, and pity; to amplify or extenuate), and in drama these sentiments should have effect even independent of theatrical representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the circumstances of the story can be simply told, sentiments must be capable of producing their effect without relying solely on staging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction of poet's and actor's responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain elements of elocution (distinguishing supplication, command, narration, question, answer, etc.) belong primarily to the player/actor and those who excel in acting, not to the poet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not blame poetry for errors that concern performance choices; the poet need not supply actor-specific modes of expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend to phonetics and organs of pronunciation in metrical composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters differ by the form of the mouth and organs of pronunciation, aspiration or softness, length or brevity, and accent—circumstances principally to be attended to in metrical compositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phonetic qualities (vowels, semivowels, mutes; length, accent, aspiration) affect metre and should inform poetic composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfection of language: perspicuous without meanness
rubrics_metrics.description: The perfection of language consists in being perspicuous without meanness: proper names give perspicuity but can be mean; uncommon expressions give dignity but can become enigmas or barbarisms if overused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temper foreign words, metaphors, ornamented phrases, and other uncommon forms with common expressions so language remains clear and dignified. Excessive metaphors create enigmas; excessive foreign words create barbarism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance and moderation in diction and ornaments
rubrics_metrics.description: All the modes of expression (foreign words, metaphors, lengthening/shortening of names, ornamented phrases) should be used with moderation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overuse or affectation (absurd and ridiculous affectation) of metaphors, foreign words, or licence in metre is to be avoided; proper use yields elevated style without obscurity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aptness and formation of metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: Forming metaphors well is the greatest art and indicates a good genius; to form metaphors well is to observe the similitude of things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metaphors may be formed from genus to species, species to genus, species to species, or by analogy; use them when the relation is apt. Well-formed metaphor is not learned but inventive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match diction and word-forms to verse type
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain word-types suit particular verse kinds: compounded words suit dithyrambic, foreign words heroic, and metaphors iambic; conversational or common words better suit iambic (imitation of common discourse).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While many devices can appear in heroic verse, choose diction appropriate to the verse's mimetic aim—heroic for elevated diction, iambic for conversational tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use lengthening/shortening/changing of names for elevation, sparingly
rubrics_metrics.description: Lengthening, shortening, and changing of names contribute to elevated language and perspicuity when used properly (e.g., substituting long for short vowels or adding/removing syllables).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such devices distinguish style from common speech but must be used with restraint so as not to become affected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantity and metrical constraints cannot be arbitrarily violated
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantity (measure) is essential to all kinds of verse; one cannot, without absurdity, lengthen syllables at pleasure to make verse out of common conversation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Licences in metre must not be abused; maintain metrical integrity even when exercising allowed liberties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic must retain dramatic form and unity of action
rubrics_metrics.description: Even in narrative imitation (epic), fables should have dramatic form and relate to one entire and complete action with a beginning, middle, and end; it should produce its peculiar delight and not follow mere history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epic may include many episodes and extend length for magnificence, but should focus on a coherent action (select a part of the larger subject) so unity and comprehensibility are preserved (example: Homer selects parts of the Trojan War).

rubrics_metrics.name: Select appropriate scope to avoid confusion or satiety
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not attempt to include every event of a large subject in one composition; excessive sameness in events causes satiety in tragedy, while epic may use variety and episodes to sustain interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a manageable portion of the story for dramatic treatment; epic narration can introduce episodes from other parts to adorn the poem without compromising unity.
